question: to the Commission Beatrice Timgren (ECR) Subject:

In the light of the ongoing discussions1 on the implementation of the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive2, the directive introduces an extended producer responsibility (EPR) scheme requiring, among other things, producers of medicinal and cosmetic products to cover at least 80 % of the costs for removing micropollutants from urban wastewater. The Commission has itself acknowledged significant divergences in the available figures and referred to updated and additional studies3. Therefore, questions arise as to whether attributing micropollutant loads to specific sectors fully reflects actual emissions and whether limiting the scope to two product groups is consistent with proportionality and competitiveness considerations. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.

the specific data and methodology on which it bases the attribution of micropollutant loads to the sectors listed in Annex III, and how it ensures that this attribution reflects actual emissions rather than product categorisation?
how it will ensure, in the context of implementing and delegated acts, that sectors with comparatively low contributions are not subject to disproportionate financial burdens?
whether it envisages a future evaluation or possible revision of Annex III should new evidence indicate that there is a mismatch between attributed and actual contributions?

https://oeil.europarl.europa.eu/oeil/en/procedure-file?reference=2026/2652(RSP). Directive (EU) 2024/3019 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 concerning urban wastewater treatment (OJ L, 2024/3019, 12.12.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/3019/oj). https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/CRE-10-2026-03-25-ITM-016_EN.html.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission’s impact assessment1 accompanying its proposal for a recast Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive2 built on the publicly available report ‘Feasibility of an extended producer responsibility system for micropollutants’3. The methodology and its limitations, as well as all relevant sources are presented therein. The report uses the chemicals list – Total Pollution Proxy Substances4 – which is available online. In line with the Directive, the producer responsibility organisations will determine how each producer contributes to the costs of quaternary treatment according to what they place on the EU market and by taking into account the quantity and hazardousness of the substances contained in their products. Producers can be exempted from extended producer responsibility (EPR) obligations if they fulfil the conditions described in Article 9.2 of the Directive. In addition, national authorities should consider the possible impacts of the EPR on the accessibility, availability and affordability of products at national level, as well as the possible impacts on the level playing field5. The Commission will first evaluate the Directive by 2033, and then by 2040, taking into account the experience gained through its implementation, the data resulting from the monitoring obligations on micropollutants, improved knowledge on the presence of micropollutants in urban wastewater, and their impacts on the environment and public health. That evaluation will include an analysis of the possible need to adapt the list of products to be covered by EPR and to revise the conditions for exemption from the EPR system (Article 9.2.a).
